content:
Many Muslims say that Paul invented Christianity; many Christians say he only explained what Jesus taught. Both claims are too simple. Paul was not the first believer, and he says he received some of what he taught. Yet the doctrines that divide Christians from Muslims are set out, in their earliest written form, in his letters.

Seven letters are accepted by nearly all scholars as Paul's own: Romans, 1 and 2 Corinthians, Galatians, Philippians, 1 Thessalonians and Philemon. Later doctrines should not be read back into them, and they should not be credited with ideas he inherited.

This article aims to provide context to Paul's influence, insha'Allah, in six teachings from those letters, each set beside the Quran. The Quran gives the measure for all six: "Christ Jesus the son of Mary was (no more than) a messenger of Allah" (4:171).[1]

"We maintain therefore that a man is justified by faith apart from the works of the law" (Romans 3:28).[2] The sentence became the banner of the Reformation, and Protestant, Catholic and Orthodox churches still read it differently. Scholars argue over whether Paul's "works of the law" means good deeds in general or the marks of Jewish identity such as circumcision.

Islam also places salvation in God's mercy. The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "There is none whose deeds alone would entitle him to get into Paradise", and, asked about himself, "Not even I, but that my Lord wraps me in Mercy."[3] The Quran never sets faith against deeds, and it asks no faith in another man's death. We set out the tension between Paul and James in Paul and James on faith and works.

"Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures" (1 Corinthians 15:3). "Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law, having become a curse for us" (Galatians 3:13).[2] Paul says he received the first of these from others, and Mark has Jesus give "his life as a ransom for many" (Mark 10:45), so the idea is older than his letters. His letters gave it the shape the churches built on.

The Quran denies the event and the doctrine. Of Jesus: "they killed him not, nor crucified him, but so it was made to appear to them" (4:157). Of sin: "no bearer of burdens can bear the burden of another" (6:164). Of forgiveness: "Despair not of the Mercy of Allah: for Allah forgives all sins" (39:53).[1] We set out the question in does God require blood to forgive?

"Therefore as sin entered into the world through one man, and death through sin; and so death passed to all men, because all sinned" (Romans 5:12). "For as through the one man's disobedience many were made sinners, even so through the obedience of the one, many will be made righteous" (Romans 5:19).[2] Augustine, centuries later, built the Western doctrine of original sin on these verses; the Orthodox churches never accepted all of it.

The Quran tells Adam's sin and its end in two verses: "Then learnt Adam from his Lord words of inspiration, and his Lord Turned towards him" (2:37), and the couple's own prayer, "Our Lord! We have wronged our own souls" (7:23).[1] Adam repented and was forgiven, and no child inherits his guilt. We set out the doctrine in original sin.

Paul calls the Law "holy, and the commandment holy, and righteous, and good" (Romans 7:12), and calls Christ "the fulfillment of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes" (Romans 10:4).[2] The Greek telos there can mean goal or end, and Christians still argue which. In practice his churches kept neither the food laws nor circumcision.

The Quran accepts that laws change between prophets: "To each among you have we prescribed a law and an open way" (5:48).[1] The change it accepts comes by revelation to a prophet. The dispute with Paul is over whose authority set the Law of Moses aside. We set out his record on the Law in Paul and the Law and on circumcision in Paul and circumcision.

Paul writes that Christ, "existing in the form of God", was exalted so "that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow ... and that every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father" (Philippians 2:6 to 11). He sets "one God, the Father" beside "one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things" (1 Corinthians 8:6).[2] These verses became the base of the later creeds, though the doctrine of the Trinity was defined only at Nicaea in 325 and after.

The Quran honours Jesus as Messiah, a Word from God and a messenger, and refuses him divinity: "Say not 'Trinity': desist: it will be better for you: for Allah is one Allah: Glory be to Him: (far exalted is He) above having a son" (4:171).[1] We set out the Quran's case in 5 reasons why Muslims believe that Jesus is not God.

"There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free man, there is neither male nor female; for you are all one in Christ Jesus" (Galatians 3:28).[2] Paul's mission made the movement Gentile, and within a few generations it stood apart from Judaism.

Islam is also open to every people: "We created you from a single (pair) of a male and a female, and made you into nations and tribes, that ye may know each other" (49:13).[1] Its unity rests on worship of God alone, with no union with the death of another. Apostle of Doom sets out how far Paul's doctrines reshaped the faith in seven doctrines.

The bottom line

Paul did not invent every Christian belief; he received some and says so. His letters gave the earliest written form to six teachings that became the core of Christian doctrine: justification by faith, atonement by the death of Jesus, Adam's sin passed to all, the Law set aside, Jesus exalted above every name, and Gentiles brought in without the Law.

Each of the six meets a Quranic answer: mercy without a sacrifice, no bearer of another's burden, Adam forgiven, law changed only by revelation, Jesus a messenger and no more, and one faith for every people in the worship of one God. The difference between Paul's gospel and the Quran's account of Jesus is a difference of substance, and the Quran gives it in Jesus' own words: "worship Allah, my Lord and your Lord" (5:117).[1] Allahu alam.

Notes

  1. Quran 2:37; 4:157; 4:171; 5:48; 5:117; 6:164; 7:23; 39:53; 49:13, translated by A. Yusuf Ali.
  2. Romans 3:28; 5:12; 5:19; 7:12; 10:4; 1 Corinthians 8:6; 15:3; Galatians 3:13; 3:28; Philippians 2:6 to 11; Mark 10:45 (World English Bible).
  3. Sahih Muslim, Book of the Characteristics of the Day of Judgement, Paradise and Hell, the report of Abu Hurayra on deeds and mercy.
